questions.stem: A dispatcher's test rig drives a sprung cab of mass 2.0 kg on springs of 790 N per metre. What is the natural frequency in hertz?
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is the square root of 790 / 2.0, about 19.87 rad per second, which is 3.163 Hz once divided by 2 pi. Driving at that rate puts the shaker on the peak of the response curve.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Effective length of a pendulum with a bob of finite size
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the effective length of a finite bob is measured
questions.stem: A dispatcher is timing a pendulum signal on a platform. Explain how the effective length of the pendulum should be measured when the bob has a finite size.

answer.exemplar: For a simple bob the pendulum behaves as a point mass hanging at the end of a massless string, but a real bob of finite size has its own mass distributed over its volume. The centre of mass of that bob sits below its geometric centre, and the correct length for the period formula is the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass of the whole system, not the distance to the bottom of the bob. Using the bottom of the bob therefore makes the predicted period too long.

questions.explanation: A finite bob has its centre of mass below its geometric centre, so the effective length is measured from the pivot to that centre of mass. Measuring to the bottom of the bob overstates the length and predicts too long a period.
questions.hint: Measure to the centre of mass, not the bob's base.

questions.topic: Support excursion of two pendulums beating in step
questions.learningObjective: Describe the beat observed from two slightly different pendulums
questions.stem: Explain what a dispatcher would observe when two pendulums of slightly different lengths are suspended from the same moving carriage.

answer.exemplar: Each pendulum has its own period, and the slight difference means their relative phase drifts steadily, so they move together, then drift apart, then come back together, repeating with a regularity set by the small difference between their periods. The interval between successive moments of alignment is the beat period, which is the reciprocal of the difference in their frequencies, so pendulums that differ only slightly beat very slowly while those that differ more beat faster.

questions.explanation: Different lengths give slightly different periods, so the phase difference drifts and the pendulums repeatedly fall into and out of step. The slow beat has a period set by how far apart the two natural frequencies are.
questions.hint: Think about two slightly different frequencies overlapping.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Density cancels from the period of a liquid column
questions.learningObjective: Explain why density cancels from a liquid column period
questions.stem: Explain why the density of the liquid does not appear in the period of oscillation of a liquid column in a tube.

answer.exemplar: When the liquid is displaced and released, the restoring force comes from the excess weight of the displaced column of liquid, which is proportional to the density times the displacement times the cross-sectional area. The inertia of the moving liquid is also proportional to the density times the column length and the area, so the density appears once in the numerator and once in the denominator and cancels. The period therefore depends only on the column length and the acceleration due to gravity.

questions.explanation: Both the restoring force and the inertia of the moving liquid are proportional to the density, so the density cancels from the ratio that sets the period. The period depends only on the column length and gravity.
questions.hint: Look for the density in both the force and the inertia.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why energy alternates twice in each motion cycle
questions.stem: Explain why the energy of a simple oscillator alternates between kinetic and potential twice in each cycle of the motion.

answer.exemplar: During one complete oscillation the mass travels from one turning point to the other and back again. It passes through the equilibrium position twice, once with its maximum velocity going one way and once with its maximum velocity going the other, and at each turning point the kinetic energy is zero while the stored elastic energy is at its maximum. Between those turning points the two forms of energy exchange, so the energy passes from kinetic to potential and back twice in every cycle of the motion.

questions.explanation: The mass reaches a turning point twice in each cycle, and each turning point is a full exchange between kinetic and stored energy. The energy therefore completes two exchange cycles for every cycle of the motion.
questions.hint: Count the turning points in one motion cycle.

questions.stem: An oscillator has a quality factor of 250 and stores 80 J at the peak of its swing. What energy in joules is lost in one cycle?

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Driving an oscillator exactly at its natural frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain the large steady amplitude produced at resonance
questions.stem: Explain why driving an oscillator at its natural frequency produces a much larger steady amplitude than driving it at other frequencies.

answer.exemplar: Energy can only be handed to a system efficiently when the drive pushes in step with the motion, which happens when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system. At that rate the work done by the drive on each swing is positive and is not given back on the return, so the amplitude grows until the energy lost to damping in one cycle matches the energy added. At any other frequency the drive gives back as much as it takes and the steady amplitude stays small.

questions.explanation: At the natural frequency the drive acts in step with the motion, so energy accumulates until damping balances it, giving a large steady amplitude. Away from that rate energy is returned as readily as it is taken.
questions.hint: Energy must arrive in step with the motion.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Natural frequency of a spring oscillator stated as a frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between hertz and radians per second
questions.stem: Explain the difference between the natural frequency of an oscillator expressed in hertz and the same quantity expressed in radians per second.

answer.exemplar: A frequency in hertz counts whole cycles of the motion each second, while an angular frequency counts radians turned per second. Because one complete cycle of simple harmonic motion corresponds to a turn of 2 pi radians, the two are linked by a factor of 2 pi: the angular frequency is 2 pi times the frequency in hertz. Mixing the two conventions is a common source of error, since a factor of about 6.28 separates them and timing calculations can be badly wrong.

questions.explanation: One cycle is 2 pi radians, so the angular frequency is 2 pi times the frequency in hertz. Stating the same oscillator's rate in the two conventions differs by a factor of 2 pi, which is easily mishandled.
questions.hint: One full cycle turns the mass through 2 pi radians.

questions.topic: Superposition of two oscillations differing in phase
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two equal-frequency oscillations combine
questions.stem: Explain how two oscillations of the same frequency combine, and why the phase difference between them decides the size of the resultant.

answer.exemplar: When two oscillations share a frequency, their sum is itself a single oscillation of that same frequency, with an amplitude that grows to the sum of the two amplitudes when they are in step and shrinks to the difference between them when they are exactly opposed. The general relation for the resultant amplitude involves the cosine of the phase difference, which is why a quarter cycle of offset reduces the result to the root-sum-square of the two amplitudes rather than their simple sum.

questions.explanation: Two oscillations of equal frequency combine into one at that frequency, and the resultant amplitude is set by the cosine of the phase difference. In-phase signals give the largest result and exactly opposed signals the smallest.
questions.hint: The cosine of the phase difference sets the amplitude.
